Why does powder need compression in order to fire properly?
So the blast ignites the powder rather than blowing it away.
So then why does a flour cloud explode when ignited?
Because gunpowder has its own oxygen supply, and flour doesn't, flour needs to be dispersed through the air to ignite.
I think compression/enclosing the powder also redirects the heat from the reaction back into the powder to create a much faster chain reaction.
Depends on the powder. I recall green dot powder doesn't require compression.

It's a matter of maintaining uniformity from shot to shot.

If there is a lot of airspace in the cartridge, the primer - which explodes with surprising force - will throw the powder into an essentially random pattern across this space, igniting different parts of it, and different amounts of it, each time. The overall burn rate will vary and the result will be a lot of variation from shot to shot.

A slightly compressed charge will be ignited in a much more predictable way, and the burn that follows will also be much more uniform from shot to shot.

The Ignition of gunpowder, depending on the type mixed, is like any volatile chemical reaction. For example, the fuel/air mixture in an engine is typically pressurized in a combustion chamber. This is done to ensure the maximum burn throughout the chemical mixture is achieved. By pressurizing the chemicals before ignition you ensure the maximum possible energy transfer to mechanical energy is as efficient as possible.
